column2: The goal: find the profit that will repeat next year too.
Set aside gains from selling land or shares, or gains from the dollar going up; these won’t repeat.
If the company pays no tax for now because of a temporary exemption, count the normal tax (25%).
If raw materials or government royalties got dearer but it isn’t in the profit yet, count the full year’s cost.
If this year, besides your salary, you also sold your old car, you don’t count next year’s income with the money from that car.
Profit that repeats
Compare the cash that came from the company’s work with its profit. Over 3 years, above 80% of profit is good; below 50% means look more closely.
If sales grew 30% but money owed by customers grew 90%, the profit is low quality.
If the warehouse fills faster than sales grow, demand may have fallen.
With inflation, machines cost more to replace than the recorded wear and tear; part of the profit must be set aside to replace them.
A colleague who says “I make 50 million a month” but hasn’t collected 40 million of it from customers yet really has 10 million in cash.
Build next year’s profit step by step:
1. How much it sells: the average of the last 12 months, allowing for new capacity. 2. At what price: the latest monthly price, not last year’s average.
3. Work out the cost of making things from the materials-to-sales ratio. 4. Raise admin costs with inflation. 5. Subtract loan interest and tax.
6. Divide the result by the number of shares, counting the latest capital increase.
To guess a taxi’s income next year: passengers a day (volume) × the new fare (price) minus petrol, repairs and insurance (costs).
Compare profit per unit of sales (margin) with the average of the past 5 years. If it’s much higher, you’re probably at the peak of the industry’s good times.
Companies that sell commodities like steel and petrochemicals have good years and bad years; price them on average profit, not the best year’s profit.
A farmer who sold their crop at a high price this year shouldn’t think every year will be the same; they work out the average of several years.
E/P means earnings per share divided by price; that is, if you buy the share, what percentage of your money turns into profit each year.
When government bonds (Akhza) pay a high return, a low P/E alone doesn’t mean cheap.
A share’s expected return must beat the Akhza return plus a few extra percent for risk (say 5 to 10 points).
A simple calculation: (E/P × the share of profit that’s paid out) + profit growth.
If a shop costs 1 billion and makes 200 million a year, its E/P is 20%. If the bank pays 30% with no hassle, this shop is only worth it if its profit grows.
Move the sliders and see how the P/E, expected return and years to get your money back change.
The same tool is also on the “Practice” tab.
Like a bank’s loan calculator: you change the amount and interest and see the instalment.
The question: how many years until the profit adds up to the price you pay today?
Price 100, first-year profit 20 and growth of 25% a year: after 3 years 76 has added up, and after 4 years 115. So about 3.6 years.
In FIS, less than about 4 to 5 years with lasting profit is preferred. Adjust this number to the current bank rate.
If you buy a car-wash machine for 100 million and it makes 25 million a year, you get your money back in 4 years.
How many years until you get your money back?
Two companies with the same P/E aren’t worth the same. A company that makes real cash, has little debt and can sell at higher prices is worth more.
Pay a lower P/E for low-quality profit.
For asset-heavy companies such as cement and mining, the cost of building the factory again is a good floor.
But being cheap against building cost isn’t a reason to buy by itself if the factory doesn’t make a profit.
A factory that would cost 100 billion to build but makes a loss isn’t cheap even at 50 billion.
